analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to offer and help pay for health coverage, and guarantees coverage to every child born after 2002.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Finance Committee; it drew no cosponsors and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, leaving the roughly 43.6 million uninsured Americans of 2002 without the coverage it promised.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every employer with 50 or more full-time workers to offer a standard health plan covering workers and their families, with the employer paying at least 72 percent of the premium and coverage starting within five days of hire, with no denials for preexisting conditions. It would have guaranteed health coverage to every child born after 2002 through a new 'MediKids' program phased in over five years, let people aged 62 to 65 buy into Medicare, and given Medicare access to laid-off workers aged 55 to 62 who lost their job-based coverage. Low-income workers and small employers would have received premium subsidies, and self-employed people would have gotten a full tax deduction for health insurance and access to the federal employees' health plans.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would have been the uninsured — about 43.6 million Americans in 2002, four out of five of them in working families, by the bill's own findings. Every employee of a 50-plus-worker employer would have gotten guaranteed coverage regardless of health history, with the employer picking up most of the premium and subsidies for workers earning under 250 percent of the poverty line. Every child born after 2002 would have been enrolled in a new national program covering everything Medicaid requires, plus prescription drugs, with no cost-sharing for the poorest families. Older laid-off workers who lose job-based coverage, self-employed people, and adults aged 62 to 65 too young for Medicare would all have gained a way into coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 50 or more full-time workers must offer a plan at least as good as the federal employees' Blue Cross standard option, pay at least 72 percent of the premium, and cannot exclude anyone for preexisting conditions, medical history, or genetic information [S2][S3].

Every child born after 2002 would be enrolled at birth in the MediKids program, phased in by age group over five years, covering all required Medicaid services plus prescription drugs, with no cost-sharing for children in families below 150 percent of the poverty line [S2][S3].

Adults aged 62 to 65 could buy into Medicare, and laid-off workers aged 55 to 62 who exhausted COBRA coverage could enroll, financed through premiums and a new Medicare Early Access Trust Fund [S2][S3].

Low-income workers earning up to 250 percent of poverty and small employers with up to 75 workers would get federal premium subsidies paid directly to their plan, and self-employed people would get a 100 percent tax deduction and access to federal employee health plans [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Larger employers would bear the biggest cost: at least 72 percent of premiums for every worker and family, plus a part-time pro-rated share, with a civil penalty of up to 10 percent of annual wages for noncompliance. The new programs would be financed by premiums paid by enrollees — MediKids premiums collected through the tax system at 25 percent of program cost, and steep deferred premiums for the Medicare buy-in paid between ages 65 and 85 — and by a funding schedule the Treasury Secretary would have to propose consisting of unspecified progressive tax increases as enrollment grows. Insurers would also have to accept community rating, charging the same standard premium within each rating area regardless of health status.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate is costly: firms with 50 or more full-time workers would owe at least 72 percent of each employee's family premium, and employers that did not comply faced a civil penalty of up to 10 percent of their total annual wages — a burden that could fall on wages or hiring [S3].

The financing is partly unspecified: the bill directs the Treasury Secretary to propose a gradual schedule of progressive tax increases to fund MediKids as enrollment grows, leaving the tax burden open-ended, and MediKids premiums would still cover a quarter of program costs through the tax system [S2][S3].

The Medicare buy-in is expensive for its users: enrollees aged 62 to 65 pay a base premium while enrolled and then a deferred premium every month from age 65 to 85 to make up the actuarial shortfall, so early access would mean higher premiums deep into retirement [S3].

The employer mandate has gaps: employers with fewer than 50 full-time employees owe nothing, and part-timers under 10 hours a week get no employer contribution, so many low-wage workers would remain outside the guarantee [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage gains would have been enormous — a path to guaranteed coverage for essentially every child and for most workers who today can be denied or priced out — and the bill's findings lay out the human cost of going without: delayed care, avoidable hospitalizations, late-stage cancer diagnoses [S3]. But the design leans heavily on employers to pay for it and leaves a growing share of financing to unspecified future tax increases, and the generous preexisting-condition and community-rating rules would have raised premiums for healthy enrollees. The stronger objection is not the goal but the unpriced bill: no one ever scored, amended, or debated it, so the real cost to employers and taxpayers was never tested against alternatives.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2003 by a single senator, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, never marked up, scheduled, or voted on, and expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine of New Jersey introduced the bill on November 23, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
No cosponsor ever joined; the cosponsor list stands at zero [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor consideration — and the bill died with the Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].

The bill's own findings stated that 43.6 million Americans, about 17.2 percent of the nonelderly population, were uninsured in 2002, and that 82 percent of the uninsured were in working families [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 50 or more workers who would have owed the 72 percent premium contribution and faced penalties of up to 10 percent of annual payroll are better off because the bill never advanced. Insurers also kept the status quo, with no community-rating requirement or ban on preexisting-condition denials outside the existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers facing the coverage mandate

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on November 23, 2003.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; received the bill on referral
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to itself on November 23, 2003, and took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor.

against.name: Senate majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded and no second senator signed on; the only sign of support or opposition is that a lone Democrat introduced it and a Republican-led Congress never acted on it.

industries.note: All new coverage would flow through private insurance: employer plans modeled on the federal employees' Blue Cross option, MediKids children enrolled through private Medicare+Choice-style plans, and premium subsidies paid directly to insurers. Insurers would gain millions of mandated customers, though they would have to accept community rating and a ban on preexisting-condition denials.

industries.industry: Employers with 50 or more full-time workers
industries.note: They would have to pay at least 72 percent of each worker's family premium, cover part-timers pro rata, start coverage within five days of hire, and face civil penalties up to 10 percent of annual wages for noncompliance. Their interest in avoiding that cost ran directly against workers' interest in guaranteed coverage.

Those with 50 or more workers would face the same mandate, but smaller firms would qualify for federal premium subsidies and could elect to enroll workers in federal employee health plans or, for workers 50 and older, in Medicare — softening the burden.
They would get a 100 percent tax deduction for family health insurance and direct access to federal employees' health plans, closing a gap in the existing tax code.
